newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac to challenge U.S. role in Latam.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac to challenge U.S. role in Latam.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac embarks on Tuesday on a tour of five South American nations, eager to challenge U.S. dominance, boost the region's relations with Europe and rebuild France's influence in an area it has long neglected.

He will visit Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay and Argentina, the four member countries of the Mercosur customs union whose emerging economic power has become a magnet for investors, and Bolivia, which is tied to the group by a free trade agreement.

Chirac told Radio France Internationale he would plead for Latin America to stake its future on the European Union, which is already Mercosur's main economic partner and aid donor, rather than on the North American Free Trade agreement (NAFTA)linking the United States, Canada and Mexico.
"Latin America's future is not in the North-South axis, but with Europe for reasons linked to history and culture," he said.

"Its vocation is not to be a piece of NAFTA, its vocation is to be open to the world and its essential economic interests -- trade, investment, aid -- lies not with the United States but with Europe. This is already the case today..." he said.
Chirac said he would address the Latin American group's grumbles about European trade barriers on farm imports.
He is to use his visit to cocaine-producing Bolivia to urge drug consuming and producing countries to cooperate better against the scourge rather than bicker about who is to blame.
"This is a global problem...We are all responsible," he said.

In Bolivia, which has a predominantly Indian population, he will also address one of his favourite issues: the need to protect the culture and languages of "primaeval people" from the domination of the English language brought about by modern communications techniques.
"It would be a disaster for the world if its cultural heritage were to gradually disappear for the benefit of a single language," he said.

Except for Brazil, the last visit by a French president to the region goes back three decades to the late General Charles de Gaulle. Since then ties have slipped, mainly due to a series of military dictatorships in Latin America in the 1970s and the foreign debt crisis of the 1980s.
France was slow to react when economic growth returned to the region in the 1990s, letting some of its EU partners, especially Germany, get a handsome lead in trade exchanges.
Chirac, who likes to see himself as a travelling salesman seeking out areas of economic growth to try to alleviate France's record unemployment, is keen to make up for lost time.
He is travelling with a dozen high-powered businessmen who have their eyes on the Mercosur's 210 million consumers and $1,000 billion GNP.

They include the heads of Electricite de France, aircraft maker Aerospatiale, distribution group Carrefour, glassmaker and buildings material group Saint-Gobain, missiles to publishing electronics and arms group Matra, water utility Lyonnaise des Eaux and pay television Canal Plus.

Latin American diplomats say French companies are keen for a share in major infrastructure projects such as a giant waterway to link Mercosur countries, a Sao Paulo-Buenos Aires motorway and a 40-km (25-mile) bridge over the River Plate estuary between Buenos Aires and the Uruguayan town of Colonia.
Cultural ties have also waned since the years when Paris was a favourite haunt for Latin American intellectuals, artists and writers, and a haven for political exiles fleeing military dictatorship.

Chirac aides are confident the trip, his longest foreign tour since he came to power almost two years ago, will open a new page in relations. The presidents of all five countries he will tour have paid official visits to Paris over the past two years.
The conservative leader's friendly and spontaneous style should go down well with Latin Americans.

For good measure, he is pandering to one of their weaknesses by taking with him Michel Platini, former captain of the French soccer squad who heads the organising committee for next year's World Cup finals in France.
